stops.name: Medina, the death of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
stops.campa: Two years after the Messenger, her father follows him, worn out by a fever after the wars of apostasy that nearly unmade the young state he governed. He is buried beside the Prophet in her own chamber, so that the floor of the small room she was married in now holds both the husband and the father who between them made her who she is. She is not yet twenty-one, doubly bereaved, and already the community's chief living witness to the years neither man survived to explain.

stops.name: Medina, her chamber becomes a school
stops.campa: Behind the curtain of the same small room, for the four decades of life left to her, Aishah teaches. Her nephew Urwa ibn al-Zubayr sits at her side so often that he becomes the chief carrier of her memory to later generations; senior Companions who fought at Badr come to her with legal questions they cannot settle among themselves. She will pass down more of the Messenger's words and deeds than almost anyone else living, on matters of prayer, marriage, inheritance, and the small domestic mercies no male Companion ever thought to ask him about.
stops.quote: We never had a problem occur to us, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, but that we would ask Aishah about it and find that she had knowledge of it.
stops.quote_source: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3883 (graded hasan sahih gharib by at-Tirmidhi)

stops.name: Medina, she tells of the Night Journey and the washing of the heart
stops.campa: Asked by her students of the night Gabriel came for him at the Sacred Mosque — the breast opened a second time and the heart washed clean in a golden basin of Zamzam before Buraq carried him to the Farthest Mosque and beyond it through the seven heavens — Aishah gives her own report of the matter, transmitted through Ibn Ishaq: that the Messenger's body was never missing from his bed that night, that it was his spirit alone which was so carried, body and vision folded into one single truth for the faithful to hold.
stops.quote: The body of the Messenger of God was not lost; he was taken by night in his spirit.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Aishah, transmitted by Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (a thinly-chained report, alongside a like report from Mu'awiya)

stops.name: Medina, the death of Umar and the widening world
stops.campa: Umar, who as Caliph consulted her often, is struck down by an assassin's dagger in the mosque itself, and as he lies dying sends to beg of her the one thing she alone can give: the third open place in her room. She had wanted it for herself; she grants it to him instead, and he is laid beside her father and her husband, within the same small chamber that is fast becoming a grave-house for the founders of the faith. The empire the two Caliphs leave behind now stretches from Persia to Egypt, ruled by men she once watched pray in Mecca's ravines as boys.

stops.name: Medina, correcting the Companions, defending the faith of women
stops.campa: Where other Companions repeat sayings she knows to be garbled or half-remembered, Aishah corrects them without deference to their seniority, insisting the Messenger's words be carried exactly or not at all. She defends the standing of women in matters of prayer and testimony against customs she judges to have crept in unauthorized, citing what she herself heard and saw at his side. Scholars of the next generation will call her, without exception, the most learned woman of the whole community, in law, medicine, and poetry alike.

stops.name: Medina, unrest under Uthman, her open disapproval
stops.campa: As Uthman's rule hardens and complaints multiply against favoritism shown to his kinsmen, Aishah joins her voice to the Companions troubled by the direction of the state, though she takes no part in violence. She is said to hold up a sandal and a lock of hair of the Messenger before a gathered crowd, reminding them how recently he walked among them and how far the community has already strayed from the plainness of those early years. Her words carry weight precisely because everyone in Medina still remembers her as his wife.

stops.name: Mecca, the news of Uthman's murder reaches her on Hajj
stops.campa: Aishah is at Mecca performing the pilgrimage when word arrives that rebels have broken into Uthman's house in Medina and killed him as he read the Quran, his blood staining its pages. The city she left in disorder is now a caliphate without a caliph, and within days word follows that Ali ibn Abi Talib has been raised up in Uthman's place by men she regards as his murderers' allies. Grief for Uthman and distrust of the new order settle into her together, inseparable from that hour.

stops.name: Mecca, the gathering for retribution, the march begins
stops.campa: Talha ibn Ubaydullah and al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, two of the ten promised Paradise in life, come to Aishah at Mecca and press her to join their demand that Ali bring Uthman's killers to justice before any oath of loyalty is owed him. She agrees, and for the first time a wife of the Messenger takes to the field at the head of men, riding out of Mecca toward Basra with an army gathered from those who share her grievance, her camel Askar carrying her curtained litter at the column's heart.

stops.name: The wells of Hawab, the dogs that bark at night
stops.campa: On the road east the column halts by night at a place whose dogs set up a sudden barking, and Aishah, asking the name of the water, is told: Hawab. She remembers at once a thing the Messenger once said to his wives — how would one of you like it, were the dogs of Hawab to bark at her — and cries out to be taken back, certain now she rides the wrong road. Talha and Zubayr bring fifty men who swear falsely that this is not that Hawab, and, half-persuaded, she lets the march continue.
stops.quote: Take me back! Take me back!
stops.quote_source: Cited in al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya (the report of the dogs of Hawab)

stops.name: Basra, the city taken and the truce that fails
stops.campa: The army enters Basra in the autumn and takes the city, and when Ali's force comes up in December it seems for a moment that bloodshed might yet be avoided: envoys pass between the two camps, and a truce is all but agreed for the following morning. But partisans on both sides who fear the truce will expose their own hand in Uthman's murder stir the camps to arms before dawn, so that both armies wake to find the fighting already begun without either commander having willed it so.

stops.name: Basra, the Day of the Camel
stops.campa: The fiercest fighting of the whole battle gathers around Aishah's camel Askar, the standard of her cause, until a ring of her own men falls one after another holding its bridle, and arrows stand from her closed howdah like the quills of a hedgehog. Ali, seeing the slaughter will not end while the beast stands, orders it hamstrung rather than her person harmed. Askar falls, the litter crashes down, and with the standard of the camel gone the whole army that had rallied around it breaks and scatters at once.

stops.name: Basra, Ali's mercy, the escort home to Medina
stops.campa: Talha and Zubayr are dead, the battle lost, and Aishah is brought unharmed from the wreck of her howdah before Ali, who speaks to her with courtesy and orders forty women of Basra's noble houses to dress as guards and escort her the whole way back, so no man rides too near the Mother of the Believers in her defeat. Her own brother Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, who fought that day in Ali's ranks against his sister's army, leads her home himself to Medina.
